en: Biographical Sketch of the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha, who translated scriptures during the Xuanzong era and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
composed by his disciple Li Hua.
The Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śubhakara possesses the pure Brahma-voice;
he should properly be called Śubhākara Saṃgha.
The *Tangyin zhengfan* (Correct Translations of Tang-Sound) states: "Pure Lion.
This is translated according to its meaning.
His name was Shanwuwei (Śīlabhadra).
He was a native of Magadha in Central India and resided at Nālandā Monastery in Rājagṛha.
He was originally of the Kṣatriya caste;
having renounced the worldly glory and nobility of a Kṣatriya,
he left the household life to follow the Buddha.
His spirit and qi were pure and void;
his accomplishments in the Way were far-reaching and eminent;
he was profoundly versed in dhyāna and wisdom.
He was profoundly adept in the gateway of the *dhāraṇīs* and the Tripitaka;
with single-minded devotion, he traveled through the various kingdoms of the Five Indias,
long spreading his illustrious reputation.
With great compassion for the benefit of living beings,
he had a karmic connection that led him eastward;
his journey eventually brought him to the borders of North India.
When the sound of the *mahācīna* [drum] resounded, our Emperor bestowed the title of "Collected Worthies and Sages" upon him and dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
This occurred in the year Kāiyuán 4, the Jǐchén year.
Carrying a great many Sanskrit manuscripts,
he arrived at Chang’an;
initially, they were deposited in the South Pagoda Courtyard of Xingfu Temple.
Thereafter, in the fifth year, the year of Ding-si (757 CE),
at Bodhimaṇḍa Temple,
he translated the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
The Dhāraṇī for Fulfilling All Wishes and the Supreme Mind: A Method for Seeking the Retention of What is Heard, in one fascicle.
Translated by the śramaṇa Siddhārtha;
compiled and transcribed by the śramaṇa Asaṅga.
Regarding the Sanskrit manuscripts brought by the Venerable Master,
an imperial edict has been issued ordering that they all be brought into the palace; however,
for this reason, we have not yet been able to translate the various sutras extensively.
In the past, the preceptor Wuxing traveled to India;
having completed his studies, he returned.
Upon his return journey to Northern India,
he unfortunately passed away.
The Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought with him—
An imperial edict was issued to welcome him back.
During his stay at Huayan Temple in the Western Capital, he took charge of the master Amoghavajra and the śramaṇa Yi-xing.
There, he selected several volumes of Sanskrit manuscripts,
all of which were teachings on dhāraṇī.
The śramaṇa Yixing...
Those [texts] that had never been translated before arrived;
in the twelfth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage into Luoyang and was stationed at Dafuxian Temple.
The śramaṇa Yixing invited the Tripiṭaka Master to translate the *Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*, one volume consisting of seven fascicles.
That sutra exists in its entirety in the Sanskrit language,
consisting of one hundred thousand verses;
that which is now being produced [is but a portion thereof].
This is merely an abridgment of the essentials.
Translated by the śramaṇa Baoyue,
and recorded in writing by Yi Xing under imperial command.
Furthermore, he revised and supplemented the terminology and principles,
balancing the refined and the plain,
so that they perfectly harmonize with the profound meaning.
He also translated the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-tantra* in three fascicles and the *Susiddhikara-sūtra* in three fascicles. As for Saṃghapāla (Sanzang),
his nature was fond of tranquility and simplicity.
He stilled his mind through meditative concentration and occasionally engaged in dhyāna-contemplation;
he encouraged and exhorted those who were beginners.
With compassion in mind,
he guides and attracts all people without fail.
Some questioned him on points of doubt;
he analyzed them with unimpeded clarity.
Whenever there were prayers for rain during droughts or for the cessation of floods, [he responded].
His arts provided great protection for the monastic community,
as detailed extensively in other records.
Later, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to his own country.
An imperial edict was issued to stop [the construction].
On the seventh day of the eleventh month in the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era,
he passed away with his right side folded over his feet.
He passed away peacefully in his meditation chamber at the age of ninety-nine,
having completed eighty years of summer retreats as a monk.
The Dharma-realm was desolate and the heart of Heaven trembled with grief;
he was posthumously conferred the title of Minister of State for Ceremonial (Honglu Qing).
He was buried on the western mountain of Longmen.
Li Xian, Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
together with the Vinaya Master Dingbin, a dignitary of the Buddhist community, [oversaw the rites].
He supervised the funeral rites;
on the eighth day of the eighth month,
he was buried at the western mountain of Longmen.

The entire capital wept in longing; the mountains and rivers changed their hue. Epitaph and Preface for the Late Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India at Dàshèngshàn Temple in the Eastern Capital of the Great Táng. Composed by the disciple Lǐ Huá, formerly Left Assistant in the Palace Library of Vòuxùn; calligraphed by the Śramaṇa Jiàichéng of Chángqìng Temple in the Hén Prefecture; with the temple’s Śramaṇa Héngxiù engraving the title characters. It is said that our Master was the true heir of the Dharma-kings of India. His lineage was pure and his realization profound. He arrived in the Middle Kingdom during the Kaiyuan era of the Great Táng, bringing with him the profound and subtle teachings of the *Vajraśekhara* and other esoteric scriptures. The Emperor Xuanzong bestowed upon him the title "Tripitaka Master" and honored him with the purple robe. He translated the *Mahāvairocana-sūtra*, the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*, and other works, totaling over one hundred fascicles. His mastery of the Sanskrit language was peerless, and his skill in ritual practice was unsurpassed. He guided the sovereign and the ministers, establishing the foundation for the prosperity of the state. His influence extended throughout the four seas, and his fame reached the eight directions. In the second year of the Tianbao era, he fell ill and passed away on the twenty-third day of the third month. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of Universal Wisdom" (Púzhì Dàshī). The Empress Dowager and the Empress also each sent gifts of silk and tea. The people of the capital mourned as if the world had ended; they wailed until their voices were hoarse, and the grief of the commoners was as deep as that of the nobility. The Master was originally from the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Central India. His secular surname was Śīla, and his given name was Prajñā. His father was the Brahmin Sthiramati. From childhood, the Master possessed a noble character; he was diligent in his studies and excelled in both internal and external learning. At the age of twenty-one, he received full ordination. He traveled extensively through various kingdoms, seeking out the most eminent masters to receive the transmission of the Vinaya and the Abhidharma. Later, he encountered the great master Vajrabodhi, from whom he received the secret mantras and the methods of the Vajrayāna. He practiced them assiduously until he attained spiritual efficacy. During the Kaiyuan era, he came to Chang'an. The Emperor summoned him to the palace to perform rites for the protection of the state. He subsequently traveled to the eastern capital, where he resided at Dàshèngshàn Temple. There, he translated the aforementioned scriptures and propagated the Dharma. His disciples numbered in the thousands, all of whom followed his instructions with reverence. Now, the Master has departed this life. To commemorate his virtue and ensure his legacy endures, I have composed this epitaph. May it serve as a mirror for future generations and a beacon for those who follow the path. [The inscription concludes with verses of praise. May the merit of this work cause the Dharma to flourish eternally and the nation to enjoy peace and prosperity. May the Master’s spirit rest in tranquility within the realm of the Buddhas. *Note: This text is a transcription of the original Chinese inscription, rendered here in English to preserve the meaning and structure.*
His name was Śubhakarasiṃha.
He was a descendant of King Amṛtodana, the paternal uncle of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
His ancestors originally came from Central India;
they divided the kingdom of Yan-tu,
and his father was King Buddhahasta.
Because the Upādhyāya was born with a noble bearing and had early on combined virtue with artistic skill,
he was subjected to successive trials.
At the age of ten, he presided over the precepts; at thirteen, he succeeded to the throne.
When his elder brothers raised armies and incited rebellion, he was compelled to campaign against them.
He received sword-blades upon his body and withstood the wheel that wounded his head;
thus the army was victorious through compliance.
Out of love for his brother,
he informed the mother-queen and addressed the assembly of ministers, saying:
Previously, when you were newly summoned to serve,
you severed affection for the sake of righteousness;
now that you have yielded the kingdom, you have fulfilled your duty.
He carried out his aspirations and,
having yielded his position to his elder brother,
resolutely sought to enter the Way.
The Empress Dowager compassionately granted her consent and bestowed upon him the Imperial Heirloom Jewel.
He traveled south until he reached the seacoast.
He attained a preeminent temple,
entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*,
and built a stūpa by gathering grains of sand.
He vowed to travel ten thousand regions;
though a black snake bit his finger, he did not retreat.
He rested his body by embarking upon a merchant vessel.
He traveled to Central India,
where he practiced meditation and recitation in secret;
light of a white hue issued from his mouth.
For three days there was no wind,
yet the boat traveled ten thousand *li*. There,
he encountered a band of pirates along with the other merchants.
On the verge of abandoning his life's mission,
he then comforted his companions and silently recited the mantras.
The seven koṭis of honored ones manifested their physical forms in their entirety;
the bandits were subsequently slaughtered by their enemies.
The invaders then exposed their crimes and submitted in sincerity;
he pointed out the paths through both the level and the perilous,
traversing the most remote and desolate wilderness.
Having crossed the Poisonous Waters,
he reached the borders of Central India and there encountered its king.
The King’s consort was the Elder’s sister; although the Elder dressed like an ordinary person, his followers treated him with the etiquette due to a sovereign.
When the King asked for the reason for this, he received his explanation.
How insufficient are words of praise!
The retinue of Bodhi returns together this very day.
The compassionate clouds spread their shade,
and the entire realm truly undergoes transformation;
therein, the treasuries of the Three Vehicles are revealed.
He thoroughly investigated the tenets of all schools;
regarding the chapters, verses, and phrases,
there was nothing he could not recite from memory.
He expounded the principles of the Dragon Palace and attained the lion’s yawn;
his fame resounded throughout the Five Indies.
The Venerable One is the foremost;
Nālandā Monastery is the fountainhead of the Semblance Dharma.
It is a great metropolis of the various sages;
there, he gathered precious jewels to adorn the forehead of the Great Image.
By day it was like the crescent moon,
and by night it radiated light.
Among the Jewel of the Sangha was Dharmakūṭa.
In the Tang language, his name is Dharmapāla.
He holds the secret key to the gateway of meditative concentration and wears the esoteric seal of the Tathāgata.
His countenance appeared as if he were forty years old,
yet eight hundred years had already passed;
he then prostrated his head at the two feet [of the Buddha].
On behalf of his own teacher, the Upādhyāya, [he] saw that the contents of the teacher’s bowl were not the food of his own country;
he then showed it to a Chan monk.
The Chan monks were people of the Hua (Chinese) ethnicity;
they saw that the oil cakes were still warm and the millet rice was left lukewarm.
Startled, he sighed and said,
"The Middle Kingdom is one hundred and eight thousand li from here;
yet they were ripe there in the morning and arrived here at noon."
"How is this so swift?
everyone in the assembly was utterly astonished;
only the Venerable Master remained silent.
The Master [Kāśyapa Mātanga] spoke privately to the Upādhyāya, saying,
"In the Middle Kingdom, at the Baima Monastery,
a multi-storied pavilion has recently been completed."
"I have just accepted an offering and am returning.
That you were able to remain silent is truly worthy of emulation."
Thereupon, he was granted the sublime teachings of the dhāraṇīs;
surrounded by nāgas and devas,
they stood densely arrayed before his eyes.
The immeasurable mudrās were received all at once;
on that very day, he was consecrated.
He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans,
and is titled the Tripitaka Master.
The Tripitaka has six meanings.
Internally, it consists of concentration, precepts, and wisdom;
externally, it consists of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
All of these are comprehensively subsumed by means of dhāraṇīs.
The dhāraṇī is the swift wheel,
the ocean of liberation and auspiciousness.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from this gate; indeed,
it is that which has been transmitted through the illumination of wisdom.
It is but a single lamp;
yet as the faculties differ and their natures vary,
the lamps are likewise infinite.
From this, there arise ten billion Śākyamunis and atom-like samādhis;
the Bodhisattva, by means of the vajra—
Comprehensively encompassing all meditative concentrations,
the white moon and the dark are identical within the Dharmakāya;
one thus ascends the stages instantaneously.
It is adjacent to the Great Enlightenment;
such are its characteristics.
The Upādhyāya paid homage to all the sacred sites.
He traveled through the vast wilderness of Huishuan,
never regretting the hardships;
he arrived at each destination three times.
He shaved the hair of Kāśyapa and received the touch of Avalokiteśvara’s hand upon his head;
he once observed the summer retreat on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There was a fierce beast ahead on the path;
he entered a cave deeply,
and the interior of the cave was as bright as day.
He beheld a standing image of the Muni,
with attendants on his left and right whose physical features appeared as if they were alive.
In Central India there was a great drought;
they sought out the Upādhyāya to pray for rain, [saying],
"O Great Sage Avalokiteśvara."
Within the lunar disc,
he holds a kamaṇḍalu in his hand and pours water onto the ground.
I was choked with emotion beneath the twin trees.
When asked about those who lived during the Buddha’s lifetime, they would not speak;
yet from ten such accounts, I have heard one.
He cast metal in the shape of palm leaves upon which the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra was inscribed,
and he melted silver to fashion a stūpa.
His physical marks were equal to those of a Buddha.
When the Empress Dowager learned that the Upādhyāya had passed away,
her tears dried up and she lost her sight.
When he sent a letter of inquiry regarding his well-being,
[the recipient] responded with clear lucidity as before.
After the Great Hero had passed into extinction...
The non-Buddhist paths are like a forest;
among the ninety-six schools,
each is devoted to its own view, and the Upādhyāya follows according to their respective attachments.
I humbly accept your instructions that shatter my doubts,
which have untied the bonds of heterodoxy at the gate of emptiness and returned me from the ford of delusion onto the path of awakening.
The Dharma-clouds bestow their moisture equally upon both the great and the small;
the waters of meditative concentration fill every vessel, whether square or round.
Thus, they topple the banners and drums of heterodox schools.
Raise the supreme banner of the Mind-King,
so that through mindfulness one may restrain the wild; thus,
in this very body, contemplate the Buddha.
The Master rejoiced and said,
"Good son, there is a karmic affinity in the Middle Kingdom; you may go there."
He then took his leave with his head bowed and traveled eastward.
While passing through the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he crossed a river in the middle of the night;
there was neither boat nor bridge upon the river.
He floated through the air to provide assistance.
The recipient said to the elder,
"An Arhat has descended."
"I am a sage of the Hīnayāna, while you,
Great Virtue, are a Bodhisattva who has ascended the stages (bhūmi).
You have thus yielded your seat to honor me as your Upādhyāya and presented me with this fine robe."
He then ascended into the air and departed,
arriving at the kingdom of O-chang,
where white mice circled around him.
Every day he offered gold coins;
he expounded the Vinaya in the court of the Turks,
and the Khatun requested the Dharma.
He then sat in meditation beneath a tree;
the Dharma appeared as golden characters,
arrayed in the sky.
Among the palace attendants of the Turks,
there was one who pressed her breasts with her hands;
the milk flowed forth in three streams and entered the mouth of the Upādhyāya.
He then joined his palms, composed his countenance, and said,
"This was my mother in a previous life;
I mistakenly raised my blade and struck her three times."
His limbs remained unhurt;
the one who hacked at him heard only the sound of copper.
He then arrived at a great lake at the foot of the Snowy Mountains.
Yet the Master’s illness did not abate.
His own teacher came from the void and said,
"The body of a Bodhisattva is identical to that of the mundane world."
"You do not abandon birth and death;
you have long since been free from all marks—
how could you possibly be ill?"
Having finished speaking, he ascended into the sky;
[the patient] was then immediately cleansed and cured.
The route led through the territory of Tibet.
He stayed in the same encampment as a caravan of merchants.
The barbarians, greedy for goods,
led their hosts to surround him on all sides.
He then secretly bestowed the Mind-Seal (cixin) upon him;
the local chieftains subsequently requested his forgiveness.
He then arrived at the western frontier of the Middle Kingdom.
At night, a deity appeared and said:
"To the east of here is not the realm of your disciple, Mañjuśrī."
He protected the Central Plains;
he passed away after paying homage at [the Buddha's] feet,
carrying the scriptures on a camel.
Upon reaching the river crossing at Xizhou,
a dragon caused the camel’s feet to sink,
and it was submerged beneath the spring.
The Master then entered the spring for three days;
he stayed in the Dragon Palace to transform it,
and the camel was pulled out onto the shore.
The Sūtra is free from leakage or dampness. Emperor Ruizong’s Way was honored and his virtue flourishing;
he mysteriously harmonized with the Unconditioned and issued an edict for the monk Yanajña and General Shi Xian.
Beyond the Yumen Pass, they waited for the arrival of those who manifest in auspicious form.
When the Kaiyuan era rose once more, the Great Transformation was renewed; the Sage Emperor dreamed of meeting a high monk.
His appearance was extraordinary;
he personally took up the brush and ink to depict it upon the palace walls.
When the Venerable Monk arrived,
his presence accorded perfectly with the dream; the Emperor’s spiritual majesty was thus manifested,
and he received him with reverence and joy.
Adorning the inner sanctuary,
the Honored One serves as the Teacher;
from the time of Śākyamuni onwards.
All knelt upon their mats and held up their vessels.
The Great Being, the Guest, was seated in the Celestial Palace;
he took his place at the Brahma assembly before the Imperial Throne.
He honored the National Preceptor,
employing the Way of Guangcheng to lead the sovereign to the vehicle of the Tathāgata.
This sublime Dharma-gate flourishes here;
there are those with skillful arts who hold the talismanic bond of ghosts and spirits.
To test his mastery of transformative powers,
he was summoned before the Imperial Presence to display his spiritual wonders; yet the Venerable remained serene and unmoved.
Yet for those practitioners, there was no application of hands or feet;
as for the remaining secrets,
none have heard of them in later generations.
Having been repeatedly requested to reside outside the palace, he was successively welcomed by various monasteries.
Accompanying the imperial entourage to the capital of Luoyang, he was decreed to be stationed at Shengshan Monastery.
From the time he departed from the inner quarters, [he lived there].
Monastics and laypeople alike gazed upon him with reverence;
people from both the Han and the barbarian tribes flocked to him. When the Upādhyāya presided over them, he treated the noble and the humble with equal impartiality.
For those who revere his exemplary form,
the lotus blossoms within the field of their vision; for those who receive his spoken teachings, [the lotus blossoms within the field of their hearing].
The nectar of immortality descended upon the source of his mind;
transcending all, he attained self-awakening and said,
"Such a person exists!"
Among his fellow practitioners,
he held only the Venerable Ratnamati in the highest esteem,
while treating all others with the etiquette due to a disciple.
The Chan Master Yixing, in the leisure time remaining after his cultivation of samādhi and prajñā,
reached the ultimate mastery of the arts as vast as heaven and earth.
If there was anything one did not yet understand, one would inquire before proceeding. The Upādhyāya was pure in character and transcendent in spirit;
his demeanor was harmonious and his speech concise.
Without relinquishing their vows,
they exercise mastery over body and mind,
yet they do not descend from their meditative seclusion.
Yet, as both their vows and power are perfected,
they respond whenever one comes;
encountering objects, they are unimpeded.
Thus, all manner of wonders were resolved;
his artistic talents encompassed those of a hundred craftsmen,
and his great compassion universally perfumed all beings.
He regards the grasses and trees as his only child;
one cannot know the limit of this sentiment within this monastery.
It is said regarding the casting of a gilded bronze spiritual stupa: "By this merit,
may you protect the world according to conditions."
His hands served as a model,
reaching a perfection unsurpassed among humans and devas.
The temple community’s casting and smelting activities were exceedingly extensive.
The courtyard was deep and narrow;
Lu feared that if the wind should rise and the fire intensify,
the disaster would spread to the monastic compound.
He smiled and said,
"There is no need for concern;
the proof shall naturally manifest."
On the day the casting was completed,
a great snowfall covered the sky;
once the miraculous stupa was finished, [the snow ceased].
Auspicious flowers drifted onto his seat;
on successive occasions he received imperial edicts,
and he brought rain to relieve droughts.
The fire was extinguished and the wind reversed;
this was clearly evident to all who saw and heard it.
He then composed himself and withdrew his request.
To provide great protection for the forest of the saṃgha,
the flourishing of the True Dharma depends upon the faith of the dragon-elephants.
He submitted a memorial requesting to return to his own country,
but an imperial edict of favor refused his request.
On the seventh day of the eleventh month in the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era.
Lying on his right side with his feet叠疊 (interlaced),
he entered nirvana in his meditation chamber at the age of ninety-nine.
The Sangha has lost one who was eighty summers;
the Dharma-realm is desolate,
and the heart of Heaven is struck with profound grief.
He conferred the title of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing).
He dispatched Li Xian, Vice Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
along with the monk Dingbin, Master of Discipline (Lishi), to serve as his ceremonial escort.
He was supervised in his burial on the western mountains of Longmen;
the entire city mourned with tears of longing,
and the colors of the mountains and rivers were transformed.
The disciple Sengbao Si was the great-grandson of Zheng Shanguo,
the Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and Duke of Xingyang.
The disciple Sengming was surnamed Wang of Langya;
both were of noble lineage and possessed superior talent.
Transcending and self-awakening,
the mind’s own speech is the eloquence of joyful exposition;
its wondrous function is the very essence of dhyāna.
He entered the master’s chamber;
there were only these two persons present.
This was in the year of Ganyuan.
He re-established the celestial order.
The Great Sovereign personally realized the compassion that is free from conditions and practiced filial piety without omission.
Thereupon, Brahmā and Śakra escorted the imperial carriage,
while devas and nāgas assisted the army;
all foulness and impurity were swept away.
Humanity and the deities were purified;
his station was entrusted with radiant light,
and the Great Teaching flourished through his singular practice.
The Second Chan Master thereupon inscribed these verses upon metal and stone;
yet the Dharma transcends words and letters.
The Way cannot be named; yet,
to comfort the hearts of his disciples who feel longing and admiration for him,
he was like Yanzi.
A Sighing Lament. Its text says: The lineage of the Sage is honored within the palace;
The Dragon supports him as he emerges from the pond; He relinquishes his throne to achieve the Way.
Teacher of gods and humans, you deliver beings as numerous as motes of dust;
You practice the compassionate breeze of ambrosia to clear away feverish afflictions, And like the moon, you shatter darkness and doubt. The Dharma is fundamentally unborn;
I now have nothing to attain. You propagate the teachings according to the regions, And have thus come to this Middle Kingdom.
The Emperor and Empress receive him with reverence; heavenly flowers fill their robes. Within the Garden of Joy, one hears only the scent of campaka.
Hundreds of thousands of millions have long since been consecrated through the taming of their minds;
the śrāvakas are present now, as majestic and sublime as the King of Mountains.
The sea-moon is full and profound; his manifestation of extinction was not true extinction.
In vain we grieve for He-lin, Yi-shui, and the Western Mountains; in the dark depths of the stone chamber, the golden coffin is already closed.
As we gaze upon this primordial day, the two Treasures continue to illuminate; the Teaching is honored and its words are profound.
Those who return to my Dharma awaken to the ultimate reality through skillful means.

The senior monk (upādhyāya) of this temple’s disciples, Seng Shanyi;

Recorded by Kenpō, Acting Junior Archbishop (Jūshō Sōjū), age thirty-eight and one. Regarding the matter of Zen Master Jōken of Mount Sōgaku, a disciple of Zen Master Gyōgi of the Unmei Gate: the recorded sayings of Zen Master Kyō of Mount Sō, a disciple of the Fifth Patriarch Dajian Huineng and Zen Master Jinsō Shinku of the Northern School, are not recorded here. Nor are the recorded sayings of Zen Master Fukaku of Mount Sō, a disciple of Zen Master Jinsō Shinku, recorded. The account of Zen Master Gyōgi at Sōyō-ji Temple has already been transcribed in the fourth fascicle of the *Tendōroku*.

One may understand its purport through the secret manual of the "Mind-Ground" (*Xindi*) as it follows the text.
Sōngshan Pují was posthumously titled Dàzhào Chánshī;
this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*.
Furthermore, Zhēnyán Yíxíng followed Dàzhào Chánshī.
Regarding the principles of the *Shouchanfa* (Method for Receiving Ordination),
those who consult the *Xiaoyao Zuyaoji* (Compendium of Essential Matters from Xiaoyao) will find that the practitioner Yixing of Songyang Temple was a fellow disciple of Wufei.
Furthermore, its purport is contained in the fifth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*, within the section on Yixing.

It was completed by Nana on the ninth day of the seventh month in the year of the Rabbit (the fourth year of the Enkyō era). The translator, Buddharakṣita, was sixty-four years of age at the time of his birth.
